subject: film
title: The Czechoslovak New Wave: comedy and dissent, 1962 to 1969
dek: In the 1960s a generation of young directors trained at Prague's state film school used a state-owned film industry to make some of the funniest, strangest and most critical films ever made in a communist country. Two of them won Oscars. Then the tanks of August 1968 ended the movement, and many of its best films were locked away for twenty years.
era: c. 1962 to 1969, with a last echo in 1970
honesty: This lesson keeps to facts documented in Wikipedia's articles on the Czechoslovak New Wave, its directors and its main films, and in the books those articles cite, especially Peter Hames's The Czechoslovak New Wave. Where sources disagree on a release year, the lesson gives the year most sources use or leaves the year out. Quotations are limited to two well-documented lines. There are no images today rather than risk pictures that do not match their captions.

timeline.label: Czechoslovak film is nationalised
timeline.detail: Right after the Second World War, a presidential decree places the whole film industry under state ownership, years before the communists take full power.

timeline.label: FAMU opens in Prague
timeline.detail: The film faculty of the Academy of Performing Arts becomes one of the first film schools in Europe. Almost every New Wave director studies there.

timeline.label: Communist takeover
timeline.detail: The Communist Party seizes power in February. Through the early 1950s, films must follow socialist realism and show heroic workers and a bright future.

timeline.label: Khrushchev denounces Stalin
timeline.detail: The Soviet leader's speech starts a slow thaw across the Eastern bloc, though Czechoslovakia's leadership loosens control more slowly than most.

timeline.label: First features of the new generation
timeline.detail: Věra Chytilová's Something Different, Štefan Uher's Slovak film The Sun in a Net and Miloš Forman's Black Peter announce a new style built on everyday life, non-professional actors and ambiguity.

timeline.label: Diamonds of the Night
timeline.detail: Jan Němec's first feature follows two boys who escape from a train bound for a concentration camp, told through memories and hallucinations.

timeline.label: Loves of a Blonde and Intimate Lighting
timeline.detail: Forman and Ivan Passer bring a documentary-like comedy of small-town life to festivals abroad.

timeline.label: The miracle year
timeline.detail: Pearls of the Deep (released in January), Daisies, A Report on the Party and the Guests and Closely Watched Trains all appear. The Shop on Main Street, made by an older team, wins the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.

timeline.label: The Firemen's Ball and Marketa Lazarová
timeline.detail: Forman's satire of a provincial committee becomes a hit at home. František Vláčil's medieval epic is finished after years of work.

timeline.label: Prague Spring, Oscar, invasion
timeline.detail: Alexander Dubček takes over the party in January and loosens censorship. Closely Watched Trains wins the Oscar in April. On the night of 20 to 21 August, Warsaw Pact armies invade.

timeline.label: Normalisation begins
timeline.detail: Gustáv Husák replaces Dubček in April. Films already finished, such as Menzel's Larks on a String, are shelved. Forman and Passer leave for the United States.

timeline.label: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders
timeline.detail: Jaromil Jireš's surrealist fairy tale is often called the last film of the movement.

timeline.label: The banned films return
timeline.detail: After the Velvet Revolution of November 1989, shelved films come out. Larks on a String wins the Golden Bear at the Berlin Film Festival.

fun_fact.title: A silent dance floor
fun_fact.text: For The Firemen's Ball, Miloš Forman wanted to record the natural voices of his mostly non-professional cast, many of them real firemen from the town of Vrchlabí. So during dialogue scenes the dance band only pretended to play, and the dancing couples wore wool socks or slippers so that their feet made no noise. The music was added later.

sections.title: Before the New Wave: a state industry and socialist realism

blocks.text: Czechoslovakia had a strong film culture long before the 1960s. Barrandov Studios, on the edge of Prague, opened in the early 1930s and was one of the best-equipped studios in Europe. In 1945, right after the war, the government nationalised the entire film industry. In 1946 the state opened FAMU, the film faculty of Prague's Academy of Performing Arts. Both decisions turned out to matter a great deal. The New Wave directors would be state employees, trained at a state school and paid with state money, which gave them studios, crews and budgets that young directors in Paris could only dream of.

After the Communist Party took power in February 1948, film became a tool of the state. Through the early 1950s, the official style was socialist realism: clear stories about heroic workers, wicked class enemies and a bright socialist future. These films were rarely popular. Audiences stayed away, and even officials came to see that pure propaganda did not work. The most admired Czech films of the period were often the ones furthest from politics, such as the puppet films of Jiří Trnka and the fantasy films of Karel Zeman, which mixed live action with animation drawn in the style of old engravings.

In 1956 Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin's crimes in a speech to the Soviet party congress, and a slow thaw began across the Eastern bloc. In Czechoslovakia, where the old leadership under Antonín Novotný stayed in power, the thaw arrived late and unevenly. By the early 1960s, though, censorship had loosened enough, and powerful figures inside the film industry were sympathetic enough, that a new group of graduates could begin making the films they wanted to make.

The New Wave was never one single style. Some directors made gentle comedies of everyday life, some made surrealist experiments and some made dark political allegories. What they shared was a refusal to make the kind of film the state had demanded in the 1950s. Instead of heroes and clear messages, they showed ordinary people who were confused, lazy, lustful, petty or kind, and they left the viewer to draw conclusions.

items: Everyday life. Forman and Passer filmed factory dormitories, village dances and family dinners, often with non-professional actors and improvised dialogue, which gave their films the feel of a documentary.
Humour, often dark. Comedy let the directors show absurdity and corruption without making a speech about it. A committee that cannot organise a dance says more about a system than a lecture would.
Experiment. Chytilová, Němec and Jireš broke up time, used colour filters, collage and dream logic, and borrowed from the strong Czech tradition of surrealism.
Literature. Many films were adaptations of Czech writers such as Bohumil Hrabal, Milan Kundera, Arnošt Lustig, Ladislav Fuks and Vladislav Vančura.
Allegory. Because direct criticism was still dangerous, several of the boldest films told stories about picnics, parties or fire brigades that audiences could read as stories about the state.

blocks.text: The movement is often compared with the French New Wave, which began a few years earlier. The differences are useful. The French directors were mostly critics who financed small films privately and often rejected tidy plots. The Czechoslovak directors worked inside a nationalised industry with full studio resources, usually told stronger stories, and made far more literary adaptations. Their main opponent was not an old-fashioned commercial cinema but a censor.

Miloš Forman is the best-known name today. The man he grew up believing was his father, a member of the Czech resistance, died in a Nazi concentration camp in 1944, and Forman grew up partly in a boarding school in Poděbrady, where his schoolmates included Ivan Passer and the future playwright and president Václav Havel. His first feature, Black Peter, follows a teenage boy on his first job as a store detective. Loves of a Blonde (1965) tells the story of Andula, a young shoe-factory worker in a town where women outnumber men sixteen to one, and her brief affair with a piano player from Prague. It was nominated for the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film. Forman wrote his Czech films with Passer and Jaroslav Papoušek, and shot them with the cinematographer Miroslav Ondříček. Passer directed his own small masterpiece, Intimate Lighting (1965), about two old music-school friends who meet again in a country town.

Věra Chytilová was the first woman to study directing at FAMU, which she entered at 28 after working as a draughtswoman, a fashion model and a clapper girl at Barrandov. Her first feature, Something Different (1963), sets the life of a champion gymnast beside the life of a bored housewife. Her second, Daisies (1966), is discussed in detail below. Chytilová worked closely with her husband, the cinematographer Jaroslav Kučera, and with the writer and designer Ester Krumbachová, one of the most important and least-known figures of the movement.

Jan Němec, whom the historian Peter Hames called the 'enfant terrible' of the movement, made Diamonds of the Night (1964), about two boys fleeing a transport to a concentration camp, based on writing by the Holocaust survivor Arnošt Lustig. His next feature, A Report on the Party and the Guests (1966), co-written with Krumbachová, is the movement's most direct political allegory. Jiří Menzel, the youngest of the major directors, made his feature debut with Closely Watched Trains (1966), adapted from a novella by Bohumil Hrabal. It follows a shy young railway apprentice at a small station in the last months of the German occupation, and mixes sex comedy with an act of resistance. It won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film at the ceremony in April 1968.

Many other directors belong to the movement. Evald Schorm made serious moral dramas such as Courage for Every Day (1964). Jaromil Jireš made The Cry (1964), an adaptation of Kundera's novel The Joke (1969) and the surrealist Valerie and Her Week of Wonders (1970). Pavel Juráček made Case for a Rookie Hangman. František Vláčil, slightly older, made Marketa Lazarová (1967), a medieval epic about warring robber clans that Czech critics voted the best Czech film ever made in a 1998 poll. Juraj Herz, a Slovak, made The Cremator (1969), a horror comedy about a crematorium worker in 1930s Prague who slides into Nazism and murder. In Slovakia, Štefan Uher's The Sun in a Net (1963) and the films of Juraj Jakubisko, such as Birds, Orphans and Fools (1969), gave the movement a second centre. The animator Jan Švankmajer also began his career in these years.

The older team of Ján Kadár and Elmar Klos made The Shop on Main Street (1965), in which a Slovak carpenter is made the 'Aryan' controller of a shop owned by an elderly, nearly deaf Jewish widow, played by the Polish actress Ida Kamińska. It won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, the first for Czechoslovakia. It is usually not counted as a New Wave film, because its style is more traditional, but its success abroad helped the whole generation.

In January 1966 five of the young directors released Pearls of the Deep, an anthology of five short films based on stories by Bohumil Hrabal, directed by Menzel, Němec, Schorm, Chytilová and Jireš. A sixth segment, by Juraj Herz, was cut for length. The film was received as a manifesto of the new generation, and Hrabal, with his talkative, drinking, day-dreaming ordinary people, became something like the movement's patron writer.

sections.title: Daisies: two Maries against the world

blocks.text: Daisies (Sedmikrásky, 1966) is the movement's wildest film. Two young women, both called Marie, decide that because the world is spoiled, they will be spoiled too. They trick older men into buying them dinner, disrupt a nightclub, cut up sausages and bananas with scissors, and finally break into an empty banquet hall, eat everything and swing from the chandelier. Neither lead was a professional actress: Jitka Cerhová was a student and Ivana Karbanová worked as a shop assistant.

Chytilová, Krumbachová and Kučera built the film out of constant changes of colour filter, jump cuts, collage and sound effects, such as the creak of an unoiled hinge when the two women move like dolls in the first scene. Chytilová said she wanted to hold the audience back from simply enjoying the characters, so that they would think about the idea instead. Krumbachová said the two Maries were a pair of silly young girls 'but they could just as well have been two generals.' Critics today read the film as a satire of consumerism, of a society obsessed with order, and of the roles assigned to women. It opens and closes with wartime footage of bombing, and it ends with a dedication to those who get upset only over a trampled bed of lettuce.

Officials did not find it funny. The authorities held back its release and export, and much of the complaint focused on the scenes of wasted food at a time of shortages. After the invasion of 1968, Chytilová was effectively barred from directing features for years. She was only allowed to return after an international campaign and a letter she wrote directly to the party leader Gustáv Husák, and in 1976 she made The Apple Game. Daisies is now one of the most widely watched Czech films in the world and a reference point for feminist film history.

sections.title: The Firemen's Ball and the party that never ends

blocks.text: After Loves of a Blonde, Forman, Passer and Papoušek went to the north Bohemian town of Vrchlabí to write their next script. One evening they went to a real firemen's ball for fun. Forman later said it was such a nightmare that they abandoned what they were writing and started a new script about it. The Firemen's Ball (1967), Forman's first colour film, follows a volunteer fire brigade's annual dance. The raffle prizes are stolen one by one, the beauty contest collapses, a house burns down while the guests watch, and the ceremonial axe meant for the brigade's dying former chairman disappears too.

Forman said he did not intend an allegory, only an honest comedy, and that honesty would make the allegory appear by itself. Audiences and officials both saw a portrait of a system in which committees promise happiness and deliver chaos. Fire brigades across the country protested that the film insulted them, and Forman's team toured to calm them down. The film still sold more than 750,000 tickets at home. Meanwhile the Italian producer Carlo Ponti, whose money had paid for the colour, withdrew his support. Forman faced the possibility of prosecution for causing economic damage to the state until the French directors Claude Berri and François Truffaut bought the international rights.

A year earlier, Němec's A Report on the Party and the Guests had told an even darker story. A group of friends on a picnic are stopped in a forest by a smiling, aggressive young man and his followers, then invited to an outdoor banquet by a genial host. One guest quietly leaves. The others, eager to keep their seats, help organise a hunt for him with a dog. The cast included writers and artists from Prague's intellectual circles, including the director Evald Schorm as the guest who walks away and the novelist Josef Škvorecký. The film was banned from 1966 to 1968, released briefly during the Prague Spring and then banned again for twenty years.

sections.title: What was happening elsewhere at the same time

blocks.text: Czechoslovakia was not the only Eastern bloc country with a film renaissance. In Poland, the Polish Film School of the late 1950s, led by Andrzej Wajda with films such as Ashes and Diamonds (1958), had already shown that a state cinema could produce serious art about history and doubt. Roman Polański's Knife in the Water (1962) carried that energy into the 1960s. In Hungary, Miklós Jancsó's The Round-Up (1966) used long, choreographed takes to show power and terror in the aftermath of the 1848 revolution, and István Szabó began his career. In Yugoslavia, the so-called Black Wave of Dušan Makavejev and others made sexually frank and politically sharp films until the authorities cracked down in the early 1970s. In the Soviet Union, Andrei Tarkovsky's Andrei Rublev was completed in 1966 but not released at home until 1971.

In the West, the 1960s were the decade of new waves everywhere. The French New Wave had begun with Truffaut's The 400 Blows and Godard's Breathless in 1959 and 1960. Britain had its kitchen-sink dramas about working-class life. Brazil had Cinema Novo, led by Glauber Rocha, whose Black God, White Devil (1964) mixed politics and myth. In Japan, Nagisa Ōshima and others broke with the studio masters of the 1950s. In the United States, the old Hollywood system was collapsing, and by the end of the decade New Hollywood had begun. Two Czechoslovak directors, Forman and Passer, would soon become part of it.

The events of 1968 tied several of these stories together. In May, protests in France spread to the Cannes Film Festival, where Truffaut, Godard and others forced it to close early. A Report on the Party and the Guests had been entered in that year's competition, so it lost its chance to be judged. Three months later, Warsaw Pact tanks entered Prague.

In January 1968 Alexander Dubček replaced Novotný as party leader and began the reforms known as the Prague Spring, including a near end to censorship. For a few months the filmmakers could do almost anything. On the night of 20 to 21 August 1968, armies of the Soviet Union and its Warsaw Pact allies invaded. In April 1969 Gustáv Husák replaced Dubček and began what the regime called normalisation: the reforms were reversed, party members were purged, and culture was brought back under control.

For the film world this meant shelved films and broken careers. Menzel's Larks on a String (1969), a comedy about 'bourgeois' prisoners sent to work in a scrapyard in the 1950s, was banned before release. The Firemen's Ball and A Report on the Party and the Guests were banned. The Cremator was withdrawn from cinemas in 1973. Chytilová was kept from directing for years, Krumbachová was pushed out of the industry, and Němec was forced to leave the country in 1974.

Forman and Passer went to the United States. Passer made American films such as Cutter's Way (1981). Forman won the Oscar for Best Director twice, for One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (1975), a story of one man against an institution, and Amadeus (1984), which he shot largely in Prague. Menzel stayed, kept working within the limits allowed and returned to Hrabal again and again, with Cutting It Short (1981) and My Sweet Little Village (1985), which was nominated for an Oscar. After the Velvet Revolution of November 1989, the shelved films came back. Larks on a String won the Golden Bear at the Berlin Film Festival in 1990, twenty-one years after it was made.

The movement's influence is wide. Its mix of documentary realism, sad comedy and quiet political meaning shaped later Eastern European cinema, and its surrealist strand, from Daisies to Valerie and Her Week of Wonders and Švankmajer's animation, has a large following today. It also showed something unusual: that some of the boldest films of the 1960s came from inside a state-controlled industry, made by people who were paid by the state they were criticising.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: The Czechoslovak New Wave had more money and better studios than most independent filmmakers in the West, but it also had a censor. Did working under censorship push these directors toward humour, allegory and experiment that made their films better, or is that a comfortable story we tell afterwards about artists whose careers were damaged or destroyed?

glossary.explain: A group of Czech and Slovak films and directors of roughly 1962 to 1969, known for everyday realism, dark comedy, surrealism and veiled political criticism. Sometimes called the 'Czechoslovak film miracle'.
